title: How early New Orleans bands worked without readers
summary: Bigard says critics misunderstand Dixieland: bands had a violinist leader because few horn players could read, so others fingered their own parts by ear since whites would not teach Black players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But there's another subject I'd like to bring up while I'm at it.

I see all these critics are writing about New Orleans jazz, the Dixieland band, and all that. They don't know the half of what a Dixieland band is. See, the real Dixieland band, all of them, they had a violinist who was the leader, see. And the reason they had a violinist was because the average -- there was only about a few could read music, you know, like a trumpet player, a few good trumpet players that could read music. Very few clarinetists could read music. And trombonists -- very few trombonists could read music at that time.

So when they had a band, they had a violinist who was the leader. Like, he'd buy the music. He'd play the melody to the tune, whatever they bought, and then the trumpet player would pick up -- he'd pick up because he could play it, then the clarinet player, he'd listen and he'd put his own melody to it. So would the trombonist, see? And that's the way they formed the band, and that's how they got the melody.

But these people writing and they talk about -- they -- that's why they should give New Orleans' players a lot of credit, because in those days the whites wouldn't teach them. They wouldn't teach any colored guys to read music. They had to play it the best way they could. If they bought an instrument, they had to learn it the best way they could.
They'd finger instruments -- It's unbelievable the way they'd finger it, but they'd get the right notes. That's the greatest part about the whole bit.
